paper_title: Single-Database Rewards Are Hackable: Counterfactual Execution for Trustworthy Text-to-SQL RL

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) for text-to-SQL agents pays a query when its result matches the reference on one database. However, a wrong query can match by luck when the data lack the rows that expose its bug. We study a counterfactual-database (CF) reward that also runs the final query on a few hidden, code-generated copies of the database and pays only if all results match (strict form) or by the share matched (mean form). On 1,302 synthetic audit questions, the strict form lowers the share of buggy queries paid in full from 29.5% to 16.8% and of reward hacks from 54.1% to 1.9%, rejecting 0 of 2,847 correct queries; copies from a family-blind generator do about as well. In a controlled GRPO comparison on a 3.35B model with three seeds per arm, training on the mean form did not improve in-domain accuracy (8.4% vs 11.7%), because the two rewards disagreed on only 5-7% of rollouts; on Spider it gained 1.6 points. One seed reverses both signs, so single-seed reward comparisons mislead. Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards ; data, models, demo: https://huggingface.co/counterfactual-sql

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A text-to-SQL query that fails is visible; one that runs and returns plausible but wrong number ends up in business report. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains such agents by executing the generated query and paying it when its result matches the reference result on one database [15, 18, 22]. The check is cheap but has blind spot. Asked How many distinct customers bought grocery product in 2025?, our agent counted distinct orders. On the database it explored, each buyer placed one order, so both counts are 10 and the reward paid in full; on resampled copy where two customers placed five orders, the reference answer is 12 and the agent says 15 (Figure 1). However, execution-match rewards assume that one database separates correct from incorrect queries. This fails when the question reads small slice of the data, such as one city, year or category: in our synthetic retail databases, 29.2% of realistic buggy queries pass the single-database (single-DB) check at 50 customers, against 0.8% at 500 customers. Real questions often filter to such slices; an LLM judge would add second model that can be gamed. We ask: can grading the final query on databases the agent never sees make SQL reward harder to hack, and does training on it produce more trustworthy agent? We grade each query on the original database and two (rarely three) hidden copies, generated by code one bug family at time, and pay only if all results match. Bottom: test item where the agent counts orders (red) instead of customers (green). that cuts the full-pay rate of buggy queries from 29.5% to 16.8% and of hacks from 54.1% to 1.9% without rejecting correct query  (Table 1)  . (ii) Evidence that public rewards share the hole: an exploit in AgentTunes SQL reward (fixed upstream), and the same gap in the SkyRL-SQL reward and eight published Spider systems. (iii) controlled three-seed training study with an honest null: with only the reward changed, the CF reward did not train better agent in domain, and we trace why; it gains 1.6 points on Spider, within seed noise  (Table 2)  . Related work. Reward hacking, where an optimizer is paid through proxy that diverges from the intended objective, is well documented [1, 21, 8]. Text-to-SQL RL trains on execution-match rewards [15, 18, 22], ReViSQL finds many positive execution rewards false [26], and DualSQL tightens the comparator [5]. Test suites [25, 24], generated grading data [4, 10] and harder code tests [11] catch lucky-correct programs [17], mostly at evaluation time. We move the check into the RL reward and audit it before training. It bears on reward evaluation, red-teaming and monitoring.

sections.title: 2 Method
sections.content: Threat model. The adversary is the policy. It sees the question, schema and original database D0 (read-only), never the copies or grader. In scope: lucky-correct queries, literal smuggling (hard-coding an answer seen while exploring), hard-coded row IDs and comparator holes; out of scope: grader tampering and wrong references. Rewards. Let be the agents final query, the reference query and exec(y, D) the rows that returns on database D. Define Ck := 1[exec(y, Dk) exec(y, Dk)], where is strict multiset match of rows (ordered when the reference is ordered). The single-DB reward and the CF reward are R(x, y) := C0, R(x, y) := (cid:81)K k=0 Ck. (1) The main run trains on the mean form Rmean := C0 1 k=1 Ck, fixed before training; the curriculum run uses the strict R. Execution is sandboxed and read-only. Under GRPO [20], which normalizes rewards over prompts rollouts, the rewards of Eq. (1) differ only where pays and does not. (cid:80)K Counterfactual copies. Each copy applies one rule edit to the slice the question reads and keeps the business rules. Answer-changing edits, such as new customers in the slice, defeat literal smuggling and hard-coded IDs. Answer-preserving edits keep the reference answer but add rows that expose one bug family: an extra active order (F1, duplicates), instalment payments (F2, join fan-out), cancellations or refunds (F3, missing filters) or superseded tier rows (F4, superseded records). sections.title: 3 Experimental setup
sections.content: Data. seeded generator builds 8-table retail SQLite databases; 18 question templates span the four bug families. The audit split has 1,302 items, the training split 907, and the test split 331 from 7 templates unseen in training (214 of them F4, which no training question covers). Test items have 4 copies from different, family-blind generator; sample is verified if it matches on the original and all 4. For transfer we use the 1,034 Spider dev questions [23], with execution accuracy (EX) on the original database and test-suite accuracy (TS) on the databases of Zhong et al. [25]. Model and training. We use Tiny Aya Global (3.35B) [19] with rank-16 LoRA [12] in AgentTune [7]; the agent has one tool, run_sql on D0, and up to 5 steps. SFT uses 353 scripted trajectories and holds out 3 of 11 training templates, so GRPO sees questions SFT gets wrong. GRPO runs 60 steps on 445 prompts (6 rollouts 4 prompts, temperature 1.0, KL weight 0.02). The two arms, ( R) and (CF reward), share initialization, data and hyperparameters; only the reward differs. Seeds 02 set prompt order and the trainer RNG. pre-registered curriculum pair trains on 36 hard prompts where 89% of SFTs passes are lucky. The main pair took about 7 hours on one L4 GPU (about $5); the copies add about 1 ms of CPU time per rollout (Appendix C). Evaluation. We draw 8 samples per test item and 4 per Spider question (temperature 0.7) and report Wilson 95% intervals over samples, and paired bootstrap intervals for differences that resample questions (samples averaged per question). The primary test pools each questions samples over seeds; as it ignores training variance, we also give seed-level interval over per-seed differences.

With blind copies, the CF reward pays 16.8% of mutants and 1.9% of hacks and rejects 0 of 2,847 correct queries; literal smuggling drops to 0 of 1,302. That is 43% relative cut, short of the 50% we pre-registered. Survivors are mutants the random copy does not touch (40.0% of all_customers, 37.7% of missing_refunds; Appendix D), and every paid hack is hard-coded-ID query whose answer-changing copy kept the same IDs (54 of 235). Informed copies lower mutant pay to 1.5%, an optimistic bound. The copies need not encode our bugs, and larger database is no substitute. Copies from the family-blind test generator pay 17.2% of mutants and 2.3% of hacks (0 of 3,017 correct queries rejected); without the F4-targeted edits, F4 hack pay still falls from 54.3% to 3.7% (mutants: 28.5% to 23.5%). One database as large as the original plus two copies (150 customers) passes only 7.8% of mutants but pays every literal and hard-coded-ID hack: size catches accidents, not exploits. The CF reward did not train better agent in domain. Pooled over three seeds, GRPO on Rmean verifies 8.4% of test samples against 11.7% for GRPO on (3.2 [4.7, 1.8]) and stays at or just below SFTs 9.4% in every seed (0.5, 0.6, 1.9 points). is unstable (+3.2, 1.9, +5.3 points over SFT), so CB is 3.7, +1.2 and 7.2 by seed, each with narrow interval; seed level: 3.2 [13.7, +7.3]. The pre-registered curriculum pair (one seed) repeats the null (0.8 [1.8, +0.2]). Likely cause: weak signal. In every run 8488% of rollouts passed D0 and only 58% of passes were lucky, so the rewards disagreed on about 57% of rollouts. Lucky passes also fell under alone (seed 0: from 10.7% to 5.9% of passes) but grew on hard curriculum prompts (Appendix D). On Spider, the CF reward transfers slightly better, within seed noise. Over three seeds, CFtrained policies reach 29.3% test-suite accuracy against 27.8% for single-DB ones (+1.6 [+0.8, +2.3]); by seed the gap is +1.9, 0.5 and +3.3 (seed-level +1.6 [3.2, +6.4]). The curriculum pair agrees (+2.1 [+0.9, +3.4]). We did not pre-register this test; single-DB policies partly fell below SFTs 29.1%.

sections.title: 5 Discussion and conclusion
sections.content: Hidden counterfactual databases are judge-free check that removes nearly all constructed hacks and many buggy passes without rejecting correct queries, but changes training only where the policy is paid for bugs, rare in our runs. planted-cache pilot spread no underpaying hack under either reward (Appendix D). Audit rewards on counterfactual data first, monitor the RR gap during it, compare rewards over several seeds, and do not read passed audit as proof of correctness. Limitations and broader impact. One synthetic schema, three seeds, 60 GRPO steps, one 3.35B model, English only, no human red-team. Spider may be in the base models pretraining data. Test copies catch 54 of 103 base-blind mutants, so verified accuracy is lenient. Exploits are dual-use; we disclosed AgentTunes with fix.

What it does extra active order for existing customers new customers in the slice, with orders Edit e_dup_order e_new_customers e_zero_order_customers customers without orders e_cancelled_orders e_later_tier e_superseded_tier e_refunds e_split_payments e_split_items e_adjustments e_drop_customers cancelled orders for existing customers later tier row that changes the current tier historical tier row between the first two refunds on shipped orders, gross unchanged payments split into two instalments item lines with quantity 2 split invoice correction plus matching payment delete 30% of slice customers and their rows Targets F1 duplicates most aggregates (changing) all_customers bugs F3 missing status filter F4 latest row F4 any-row, first-row F3 missing refunds F2 join fan-out count-for-sum, fan-out F4 ignored adjustments answer-changing Item construction. An item is kept only if (1) the reference answer is not degenerate (empty, all-NULL or single 0); (2) the reference equals an independent pandas implementation on every database and every paraphrase equals the reference; (3) the reference and paraphrases are deterministic on row-shuffled copy, which catches ties and unordered LIMIT; and (4) for training and audit items, at least one answer-changing and one answer-preserving copy exist. Copy selection. The informed set adds the best answer-changing copy, then the best answerpreserving copy, then more copies while they kill more of the templates known mutants, up to 3. The blind set takes one random copy of each kind. Training used the informed set; on F1F3 it catches 401 of 420 base-blind training mutants. Test copies. Each test database is foreign-key-closed 50-customer sub-database of 500-customer parent, plus four family-blind mutations: resample sharing half the customers, clone of 25% of customers under new IDs, placed/cancelled swaps on 40% of unpaid orders, and relabeling of 30% of tier rows. The period-edge copy (audit only) moves half of years orders to January 1 or December 31 and half of the other years orders just outside the year, with their payments, refunds and adjustments.

sections.content: Constructed hacks. Literal: query that returns the reference answer as constants (1,302). Empty: query that returns no rows (1,302). sections.title: System prompt
sections.content: (verbatim; the user turn is Database: <id> and Question: <question>): {SCHEMA} You are careful data analyst working with retail SQLite database. Schema: Business definitions: Use the run_sql tool to explore the data and check your query before answering. missing business filters and superseded records. reply with one short sentence and your final query in ```sql block. The final query must compute the answer from the tables; do not hard-code values. Watch for duplicate rows, joins that multiply rows, When you are done, {GLOSSARY} Engineering fixes. Before any reported run we fixed three issues that change results: AgentTunes multi-turn token stream dropped chat-template tokens between turns (importance ratio about 105), so we re-render the conversation and train strictly on-policy; bf16 LoRA merge left 3861% of weights bit-identical to the base, so we merge in fp32 and store fp16; and an evaluation seed bug gave identical samples per prompt. Compute. SFT: 72 minutes on an RTX 5070 Ti. GRPO main pair: about 7 hours on one L4 (about $5). Curriculum pair: about 8.5 hours on one L4 (about $6). Seeds 12: about 14 hours (about $10). 9 LeakySQL pilot: about 7 hours (about $5). Test generation: about 13 minutes per model; Spider: 36 minutes for 4 models. The audit runs on CPU in minutes.
